title: The multiverse is metaphysics, not science
subtitle: What's missing in the multiverse debate
author: Quentin Ruyant
introduction: The multiverse theory has gained popularity as, among other things, a way to explain our universe’s apparent fine-tuning for life. Against the theory, many argue that while the multiverse could account for life in some universe, it fails to explain why there is life in our universe specifically. But, as Quentin Ruyant argues, both sides of this debate fail to appreciate one crucial thing: the context in which we observe life. While there are valid reasons to reject the multiverse, the “this universe” objection is not one of them.
body:
The fine-tuning argument for the multiverse

Our universe seems to be miraculously fine-tuned for life. According to physics, if the value of cosmological constants were slightly different, it would not have the same long lasting structure, and life would be impossible. How can we explain it? Perhaps God wanted there to be life, and designed our universe in this way. But here is another explanation: if there are many universes, each with different values for cosmological constants, then it’s probable that at least some of them have the right constants for life. And of course, as living organisms, we happen to live in one such universe: there’s no mystery.

This explanation is quite intuitive. We can explain in a similar way why our planet, the Earth, has some rare features that make it hospitable for life, such as having a moon that stabilizes its axis. However, some authors have objected that this kind of reasoning is fallacious. According to them, although the multiverse can explain why there is life rather than not somewhere in the multiverse, it cannot explain why there is life in this universe, since the existence of many other universes (or many other planets for that matter) does not affect the likelihood that our universe (our planet) in particular is suitable for life. The fine-tuning of cosmological constants in our universe thus remains a mystery.

This objection to the fine-tuning argument is controversial, but it remains influential. Part of its strength comes from weaknesses of the argument it attacks. The problem is that we could apparently apply the same reasoning to any contingency whatsoever. Take Shakespeare’s Hamlet, for example: isn’t it incredible that this precise sequence of words exists as a book? Well, if there are sufficiently many universes, this was bound to happen in at least one of them. So, our observation that Hamlet exists favours the multiverse hypothesis, by simple Bayesian reasoning (if a hypothesis makes your observations comparatively more likely, then it gets a credence boost). And the same would go for any random sequence of events, any particular sets of numbers obtained after rolling dice for instance: the multiverse provides an explanation not only for life, but for just any contingency. Absurd, isn’t it? Here, defenders of the “this-universe-objection” concur, and give their solution to the problem: the multiverse does not make it more likely that Hamlet exists in this universe, and this is what really needs to be explained.

SUGGESTED VIEWING A Goldilocks World With Tara Shears, Chiara Marletto, Bernard Carr, Massimo Pigliucci

This resolves the issue, granted, but is it the right way of doing so? I think not, as I will explain below.

But first, a disclaimer. I must say that I'm not actually convinced that this whole debate makes sense. I'm sceptical of the very idea that cosmological constants “could have had different values” in any relevant sense (different from mere conceivability, which we shouldn’t worry about). Theoretical constants generally correspond to the bedrock of our attempts at explaining physical phenomena. This is the point where all we can say is: “it’s like that, move on”. The constants of cosmology might turn out to have the value they have as a matter of physical necessity in light of a future theory, in which case the debate on fine-tuning will become obsolete. Or they might turn out to be the improbable result of a unique stochastic process, in which case the debate will gain its legitimacy. But the point is: we don’t know yet! Many of the robust explanations provided by contemporary physics are certainly here to stay, only to be reinterpreted by future science in a way that does not affect their overall relevance. It makes sense to take them as inputs for metaphysical inquiry. But cosmological constants are precisely what remains unexplained by physics. It makes no sense to take their existence and unlikelihood for granted in the context of a philosophical argument. In this respect, I would urge everyone to let science do its job instead of speculating in the wild.

However, let’s put these worries aside, because there are still interesting things to say about cosmological arguments in general on the basis of this case.

SUGGESTED VIEWING The laws of physics are not fixed With João Magueijo

Indexicality and Scientific Modelling

Let's pretend, for the sake of the discussion that we are in a situation where we have two competing cosmological models for explaining life. In one of them, there's only one universe. In the other, there are many. In both models, any given universe is very unlikely to permit life, but the multiverse model makes it likely that at least one universe will permit life. And we observe that there's life in our universe. Does it favour the multiverse hypothesis or not?

We can start by addressing the weakness that I was mentioning before: that the argument for the multiverse could be used on any contingency whatsoever, which seems absurd. I believe that this worry can be addressed successfully by putting forth an idea that I have developed in my past research: that theoretical models are indexical.

One important implication of model indexicality is that the predictions of models are always conditional.

A linguistic term is indexical if it only acquires concrete meaning when used in context. For example, “I” only acquires concrete meaning when someone pronounces the word, or “now” when uttered at a particular time: then they refer to the speaker and time of utterance respectively, but outside of a particular context, they do not refer to any particular person or time. Their general meaning can only be expressed by means of a rule that tells us how to interpret them in any context: what philosophers of language call a character.

I think that roughly the same goes for most theoretical models. When used to make concrete predictions in experimental applications, they can tell us something about the objects to which they are applied. They refer to specific objects and properties. But outside of concrete applications, the most we can do is explain how they should be interpreted in any relevant context. Very often in classrooms, when a model is presented (for example the model of the simple pendulum), a fictional context (an imaginary pendulum) is introduced for exposition purposes: this, I claim, is a way of explicating the character of the model.

One important implication of model indexicality is that the predictions of models are always conditional. A model tells you that if there's a context to which it applies, then you should expect this or that result with certain probabilities. Knowing whether (or how to make sure that) a model applies to a context involves a lot of experimental abilities that are not entirely encoded in scientific theories, such as handling instruments in order to produce or isolate the relevant objects in the relevant circumstances. But once we are confident that our model applies, then we can take it to describe the context and its potentialities, and in particular, what specific outcomes are likely or not. However, outside of a context, the model is just a function from context to such content. In some sense, it does not represent anything.

If the model represents a particular kind of object, this means locating the model relative to us by identifying one or several objects of the right kind (finding a pendulum). In the case of a cosmological model, this means locating ourselves within the model.

You might think that this is only true for the models that describe generic types of systems, such as the model of the simple pendulum. But what about models that describe our whole universe, as is the case in cosmology? Well, they are not very different in my view. In all cases, the first thing to do in order to derive predictions from them is to connect them with an experimental context. If the model represents a particular kind of object, this means locating the model relative to us by identifying one or several objects of the right kind (finding a pendulum). In the case of a cosmological model, this means locating ourselves within the model. This is a bit different, but in both cases, the idea is simply to coordinate an abstract representation and our concrete experience (us, here, now), so as to endow this representation with concrete relevance for us, and this must be done before drawing any conclusion.

SUGGESTED READING The multiverse is unscientific nonsense By Jacob Barandes

Back to Cosmological Arguments

What are the implications of model indexicality for the debate on fine-tuning? First of all, it invalidates this idea that any contingency would favour the multiverse hypothesis, which is a good result. Simply put, a multiverse model should not be taken to have any direct empirical implications: before drawing its implications, we should first coordinate the model with an experimental context. Then only will our hypothesis give us some expectations for this context. Imagine you witness someone roll dice and get a double six: is it more likely that this would happen under the multiverse hypothesis? The answer is no. First locate your context: you're in a part of the multiverse where someone rolls dice. Then make your predictions: the likelihood of a double six in this specific context is just as low whether there are many other universes or only one. Other universes are quite irrelevant to these particular dice. So your observations do not favour the multiverse. And the same goes when you read Hamlet.

What now about the “this-universe-objection”?

It could seem, on the surface of it, that it is validated by our rationale. First, locate a context: this universe. Then derive predictions for this context: it is very unlikely for this universe in particular to have the right constants for life, whether or not there are many other universes. Therefore, the multiverse does not actually explain why there is life in our universe. But this is a very superficial reading. The situation described, where our universe exists, but we still haven’t observed whether or not it holds life, looks nothing like any experimental context we could find ourselves in. It’s not as if we had picked a random universe, and then wondered if it had the right cosmological constants. The proper way of making inferences is first to locate ourselves within the multiverse. This means identifying a hypothetical universe that holds life, because we couldn’t exist in any other kind of universe. Then we can derive implications for this context. And if we apply this logic, then, as it happens, the multiverse predicts, quite trivially, that our universe has life.

We must assume that we exist in order to apply any hypothesis whatsoever to a relevant context. But then, no hypothesis can make it more or less likely that we exist

Another way of making this point is that we do not have access to the fundamental essence of our universe. If I handed you a map of the multiverse, you’d be incapable of pointing at one particular universe in it and say confidently “this one, it’s ours!” before even knowing whether it permits life. But we cannot reason on an undefined object. So, in order to make things more palatable, we must understand the locution “this universe” as meaning “the universe we happen to live in, whichever it is”. We must locate it relative to us. But the multiverse hypothesis does actually predict (trivially) that the universe we live in, whichever it is, has life: it must be so simply because we live in it.

SUGGESTED VIEWING The mystery of the multiverse With Michio Kaku, Sabine Hossenfelder, Roger Penrose

Model indexicality thus invalidates the “this-universe” objection without implying that any contingency favours the multiverse. The problem is that it seems to invalidate the original multiverse explanation as well by trivialising it. We must assume that we exist in order to apply any hypothesis whatsoever to a relevant context. But then, no hypothesis can make it more or less likely that we exist (to be precise, not before observations are made: the hypothesis that a bomb was defused can make it more likely that we exist at the time of our observations, because otherwise we would be dead, but in this example, it is still required that we existed before making our observations). Can’t we ever reason about the likelihood of our own existence? Can’t we ever attempt to explain it?

A hypothesis that makes it more likely that at least one context qualitatively like ours exists should be considered more credible, all other things equal, than a one that makes it unlikely.

We can still give it a try. There are various theories about how to treat self-location uncertainty, how to locate ourselves in a space of possibilities, that is, that are relevant for this kind of inquiry, since they would allow us to assign probabilities to the existence of our own context (a universe with life) under the hypotheses considered. Discussions on self-location involve a plethora of thought experiments and arguments: the sleeping beauty problem, the doomsday argument, Boltzmann’s brains… And there is no consensus on the right self-location rule. But unfortunately for defenders of the “this-universe-objection”, all options favour the validity of the fine-tuning argument for the multiverse. The rationale is quite simple: a hypothesis that makes it more likely that at least one context qualitatively like ours exists should be considered more credible, all other things equal, than a one that makes it unlikely. In the limit case, if a hypothesis makes it impossible to locate ourselves in its models, it should simply be discarded in favour of the ones that still make it possible: no one would object to this.

To sum up. First, it isn’t obvious that the presence of life in our universe really is unlikely in a relevant sense of “unlikely”. Then even if it were the case, our own existence and its preconditions do not really constitute empirical evidence per se: they rather constitute the background against which all empirical evidence is assessed. So, maybe we should just accept that there are limits to what can be known when it comes to problems like this one, and refrain from speculating. Now if we insist in assuming that there’s a problem of fine-tuning and that it can be settled by reasoning alone, then the multiverse hypothesis does provide a reasonable solution, contrarily to what objectors claim. However, at this point, we have to acknowledge that we have left the domain of what can be assessed by well-established empirical methods, and entered the muddy waters of metaphysics.
